Myths & Facts

Correcting information. Reducing distance.

HIV myths are not harmless mistakes. They can shape whether someone is respected, supported, loved, or excluded.

Myth

HIV is transmitted through hugging or shaking hands.

Fact

HIV is not transmitted through everyday social contact.

Hugging, shaking hands, or being in the same room does not transmit HIV.

Why is this harmful?

It can cause people living with HIV to be avoided for no medical reason.

Myth

Sharing food or drink can transmit HIV.

Fact

HIV is not transmitted by sharing food, water, plates, or cutlery.

Everyday impact

Refusing to share a meal can feel like rejecting the person, not simply being cautious.

Myth

You can tell someone’s HIV status by looking at them.

Fact

Appearance cannot show HIV status. Only an HIV test can determine it.

Why are assumptions harmful?

Judging by appearance, identity, or occupation creates prejudice and false reassurance.

Myth

HIV and AIDS are the same thing.

Fact

HIV is a virus. AIDS is the most advanced stage that can develop when HIV is untreated.

U=U

Myth

“A person with HIV always transmits HIV to sexual partners.”

Fact: A person taking ART who maintains an undetectable viral load does not sexually transmit HIV.

Sources

  • WHO — HIV and AIDS fact sheet
  • UNAIDS — Undetectable = Untransmittable
Last reviewed: 19 September 2026. This page provides general education, not an individual risk assessment.
